doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Eddie Condon's contribution and character
summary: He praises Condon as a bandleader who broke racial barriers at his Town Hall concerts, despite his heavy drinking. He recalls Condon hating the word Dixieland.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What’s your take on Eddie Condon as to how he fits into the history of jazz? What was his major contribution?

Oh boy. He was a great band leader. He surrounded himself with great musicians. I don’t think he gave it that much thought but he actually was in the vanguard of breaking down racial barriers. At the same time that Benny Goodman was putting on his 1938 concert which had blacks and whites in the same band, Condon had his Town Hall concerts where he was doing the same thing. I think he just believed if you could play, you could play. Don’t worry about your sex, don’t worry about your color. I think he had — and nobody is aware of the strong role he had at the time. I mean he was, you know his

personal life was in kind of a funny shambles. I mean it was sad, bittersweet, because he drank an awful lot but he loved to party, but he attracted to his club some of the world’s, I mean the great people of the world would come, the sports, they even some of them came into us, the carryover, the Condon’s that we ran. Walter Cronkite was a jazz fan. Loved Wild Bill Davison. I still correspond with him. So Condon was a very key person. I mean he grew up, he was born in Indiana and was in with those guys in Chicago before coming to New York. So he was in when swing was evolving. He hated the word “Dixieland,” and don’t ever mention Dixieland to Eddie Condon. We were just playing music. In fact one of his books it’s called We Called It Music. So he was quite a man, and he knew good jazz, he knew it too. I mean he wouldn’t tolerate mediocre, mediocrity.
